paper.title: Contributions of insula and superior temporal sulcus to interpersonal guilt and responsibility in social decisions

nodes.text: What are the neural mechanisms of interpersonal guilt and social responsibility evoked by risky social decisions?
nodes.anchor: neural mechanisms underlying guilt evoked during such situations of social responsibility are still unknown

nodes.text: Does responsibility for choosing a risky option that yields a low outcome for a partner reduce momentary happiness (a guilt effect)?
nodes.anchor: happiness decreases following low outcomes for the partner were larger when the participant rather than their partner had made the choice

nodes.text: Left anterior insula activation reflects interpersonal guilt during risky social decisions.
nodes.description: Left aIns responded more to low lottery outcomes for the partner when the participant rather than the partner made the choice, replicating prior associations between aIns and guilt.
nodes.anchor: Activation in the left anterior insula (aIns) reflected this effect, replicating previous associations

nodes.text: Participant happiness is reduced more by low lottery outcomes for the partner when the participant (vs. partner) made the choice, operationally defining a guilt effect.
nodes.description: The interaction between partner outcome and decision-maker on momentary happiness was significant in both studies, consistent with 'simple guilt' as defined in psychological game theory.
nodes.anchor: participant happiness was lower when they rather than the partner had chosen the lottery

nodes.text: Partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant choices (social_pRPE) contribute to explaining variations in momentary happiness, over and above self-related reward signals.
nodes.description: The Responsibility model, which separates partner RPEs by decision-maker, best fit happiness data in both studies.
nodes.anchor: the Responsibility and Responsibility Redux ( Figure 3C, G ) models explained the data best

nodes.text: Left superior temporal sulcus tracks partner reward prediction errors specifically when those errors result from the participant's own choices.
nodes.description: Model-based fMRI analysis (GLM2) revealed a left STS cluster responding more to social_pRPE than partner_pRPE, suggesting a role in monitoring consequences of one's own decisions on others.
nodes.anchor: this region of the left STS tracks a partner's unexpected outcomes less when they do not follow from the participant's decisions

nodes.text: Functional connectivity between left anterior insula and right inferior frontal gyrus varies as a function of choice type and social condition during social decision-making.
nodes.description: Right IFG connectivity with left aIns was highest during Risky-Solo and Safe-Social choices, suggesting IFG processes guilt-relevant information during social decisions.
nodes.anchor: Connectivity between this region and the right inferior frontal gyrus varied depending on choice and experimental condition

nodes.text: Social decision-making (choosing for self and partner vs. self only) engages precuneus, left temporo-parietal junction, and medial prefrontal cortex.
nodes.anchor: Deciding for both self and partner rather than just for oneself evoked increased activations in precuneus, left TPJ, and dmPFC

nodes.text: A left anterior insula cluster (22 voxels, peak MNI [−28 24 −4], T=3.95, d=0.59) showed higher BOLD responses to low partner lottery outcomes from participant vs. partner choices, surviving FWE correction within the anatomically defined left aIns ROI (p=0.024).
nodes.anchor: peak T = 3.95, d = 0.59, 22 voxels, peak intensity at [–28 24 –4]

nodes.text: The interaction between partner outcome and decision-maker on participant happiness was significant in Study 1 (t(1180)=3.52, p=0.0004, β=0.37) and Study 2 (t(937)=2.85, p=0.0045, β=0.33).
nodes.anchor: the interaction between partner outcome and decision-maker was significant (Study 1: t (1180) = 3.52, p = 0.0004

nodes.text: Weights for social_pRPE were significantly greater than zero (Responsibility model: Study 1 Z=2.85, p=0.004; Study 2 Z=3.26, p=0.001); the Responsibility model fit better than all simpler models (Study 1: all LR≥47.36; Study 2: all LR≥77.83, p<0.0001).
nodes.anchor: weights for social_pRPE were greater than 0: Responsibility model: Study 1: Z = 2.85, p = 0.004, Study 2: Z = 3.26, p = 0.001

nodes.text: A left STS cluster (100 voxels, peak MNI [−52 −32 0], T=4.70, d=0.53, pFWE=0.022) responded more to partner RPE resulting from participant than from partner choices.
A right IFG cluster (115 voxels, peak MNI [46 16 22], T=4.34, d=0.80, pFWE=0.020) showed highest connectivity with left aIns during Risky-Solo and Safe-Social choices.
Social > Solo decisions activated three clusters: precuneus (d=0.79), left TPJ (d=0.59), and mPFC (d=0.54).
nodes.anchor: in the precuneus ( d = 0.79), the left temporo-parietal junction (TPJ; d = 0.59) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC; d = 0.54)

nodes.text: Dot products between guilt-related BOLD responses and the Yu et al. 2020 guilt-related brain signature were overall positive (mean=5.22, median=6.97, sign test p=0.017, Cliff's Delta=0.4).
nodes.anchor: overall these values were positive (mean = 5.22; median = 6.97; sign test: p = 0.017

nodes.text: Study 1: behavioral risky social choice task with momentary happiness ratings (N=40, outside fMRI)
nodes.description: Forty participants completed three sessions of Solo, Social, and Partner conditions with happiness rated every two trials.
nodes.anchor: Forty healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22–31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study)

nodes.text: Study 2: risky social choice task with momentary happiness ratings during fMRI (N=44), with conventional GLM1 fMRI analysis
nodes.description: Forty-four participants completed two scanner sessions. fMRI GLM1 coded trial events by condition, choice, and partner/participant outcomes.
nodes.anchor: 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23–50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study)

nodes.text: Study 2 computational model-based fMRI analysis (GLM2): searching for BOLD responses correlated with Responsibility model regressors (CR, EV, sRPE, social_pRPE, partner_pRPE)
nodes.anchor: We used the model to create expected BOLD responses for each participant

nodes.text: Study 2 PPI functional connectivity analysis with left anterior insula as seed region during the choice phase
nodes.anchor: we used the left insula and left STS as seed regions for whole-brain seed-to-voxel psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analyses

nodes.text: Three-condition risky monetary choice task: on each trial, choose between a safe option and a 50/50 lottery in Solo (self only), Social (self and partner, participant decides), or Partner (self and partner, algorithm decides) conditions; lottery outcomes played independently for participant and partner; momentary happiness rated every two trials on a 100-point scale; amounts drawn from gain, loss, and mixed trial types.
nodes.description: Partner choices simulated by an expected-value-maximizing algorithm. Happiness ratings Z-scored per participant. ISIs 1–2 s in Study 1, 3–11 s in Study 2.
nodes.anchor: participants repeatedly chose between safe and risky monetary outcomes in social contexts

nodes.text: fMRI acquisition on a 3T Siemens TRIO with 32-channel head coil: T2* EPI BOLD, TR=2500 ms, TE=30 ms, 37 slices, voxels 2×2×3 mm, flip angle 90°, FOV 192 mm, PAT 2 acceleration; T1 structural at 0.8×0.8×0.8 mm; preprocessing in SPM12 (realignment, normalization to MNI, 8 mm FWHM Gaussian smoothing, 128 s high-pass filter).
nodes.anchor: Imaging data were collected on a 3T Siemens TRIO MRI system (Siemens AG, Erlangen, Germany) with a Siemens 32-channel head coil

nodes.text: Fit five temporal-difference computational models (Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility, Responsibility Redux) to Z-scored happiness ratings using exponentially decaying regressors for CR, EV, sRPE, social_pRPE (partner RPE from participant choices), and partner_pRPE (partner RPE from partner choices); compare by AIC, BIC, R², adjusted R², and likelihood ratio tests (Equation 9); validate with 10-fold parameter recovery on synthetic noisy data.
nodes.anchor: we modelled the variations in momentary well-being (happiness ratings) using computational models that considered the influence of recent reward expectations, prediction errors

nodes.text: Two-stage mass-univariate GLM fMRI analysis in SPM12: individual fixed-effects models with events convolved with canonical HRF; random-effects group tests; FWE-corrected at p<0.05 cluster-level with voxel-forming threshold p<0.001; ROI analyses with linear mixed models on voxel parameter estimates.
nodes.anchor: pre-processed functional data were analysed using a standard two-stage approach based on the general linear model (GLM) implemented in SPM12

nodes.text: Seed-to-voxel psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analysis using gPPI toolbox for SPM; seed: first eigenvariate of left aIns or left STS cluster signal; interaction regressors: seed signal × Condition (Social/Partner/Solo) × Choice (Risky/Safe); whole-brain FWE-corrected at p<0.05.
nodes.anchor: We used the gPPI toolbox ( McLaren et al., 2012 ) for SPM to run seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analyses

nodes.text: Yu et al. 2020: multivariate neural guilt-related brain signature (GRBS) from reanalysis of two neuroimaging guilt studies
nodes.description: Provides the publicly available guilt-related brain signature code (Wager, 2019 on GitHub) used for the neurometric comparison in Study 2.
nodes.anchor: A recent study by Yu and colleagues re-analysed the results of two previous neuroimaging studies of guilt

nodes.anchor: asking participants directly about which emotions they have felt during the different stages of this task would allow us to link subjective experience

nodes.text: Vary partner identities (friends, strangers, artificial agent) across experiments to test the impact of social discounting on guilt and responsibility.
nodes.anchor: Varying partner identities (friends, stranger, and artificial agent) could reveal the impact of social discounting on guilt and responsibility
